series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] fs: stamp the current time for a stale delegated ctime update
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a timing issue in inode_set_ctime_deleg() where an update that doesn't advance the ctime is skipped, but should instead record the current time to maintain visibility of delegated changes. The patch modifies the function to stamp the current time when the update does not advance the ctime.

> inode_set_ctime_deleg() drops an update that does not advance the ctime.
> That is correct when a client reports a timestamp that it advanced on its

> as utimensat() does.
>

> Assisted-by: LLM

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] nfsd: accept a backdated timestamp from a delegation holder
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the NFS server to accept a backdated timestamp from a delegation holder, which was previously ignored if it moved backwards in time. The client can report file times at every delegation return, and the server will update them accordingly. If an mtime moves backwards, the ctime is set to the current time. The patch also fixes issues with caching and attribute updates when using delegations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] nfsd: compare CB_GETATTR times against the inode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the NFS server to compare client-reported timestamps in CB_GETATTR requests against the current timestamp of the inode, rather than stale values stored in the delegation. This change prevents clients from reporting outdated timestamps and ensures that file metadata is accurately updated. The patch also removes unnecessary fields from the delegation structure and fixes a bug related to SETATTR updates for delegated timestamps.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue where applications cannot set backdated timestamps on files due to strict attribute delegation rules in NFS. The patches modify the server-side code to accept these updates by changing how the ctime is handled, allowing for improved performance in common use-cases.

This reduces unnecessary writes to cachelines, making flushes cheaper and improving performance. The patch achieves this by compiling out the non-hierarchical arrays if CONFIG_MEMCG_V1 is not set, and skipping updates on these arrays even if v1 is enabled but blocked on a particular controller. As a result, the time taken for mem_cgroup_css_rstat_flush() decreases by around 4-5% in benchmarking tests.

review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's approach and asked for more information on the workload and reclaim cycle. Suggested that aging anon alongside file may have value in certain scenarios.

review_comments.author: Bo Zhang
review_comments.summary: Provided additional context on the workload and reclaim cycle, explaining that the NOIO allocations are correct but the problem lies in the reclaim side. Described a specific scenario where the patch's approach may not be optimal.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Sep 03, 2026 at 09:03:04AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> On Thu, Sep 03, 2026 at 12:01:31PM +0800, Bo Zhang wrote:
> > We have observed some cases where memory is allocated with GFP_NOIO, so
> > we cannot reclaim any anon folios unless they are in swapcache. We can
> > end up spending more than 150 ms looping in `shrink_folio_list()` scanning
> > non-swapcache folios without reclaiming a single folio. This is pure
> > overhead.
>
> Not entirely. There is some value in aging anon alongside file, so
> that the next __GFP_IO reclaimer doesn't look at a stale list.

You're right, "pure overhead" was too strong - aging anon does have
value for a later __GFP_IO reclaimer, and I don't intend to skip it in
general. Let me describe the case in full, because the reclaim cycle
itself already provides that aging on a later pass, which is what makes
me think the trade-off here leans the other way.

> Can you describe a bit more about what you observed? What workload is
> running, maybe you have a stack trace of which NOIO requests are
> routinely getting stuck in reclaim?

The workload is app launching on Android. The NOIO allocations come from
dm-verity hash-block reads via dm-bufio, which legitimately use GFP_NOIO
because they run underneath the IO path:

  worker_thread
   process_scheduled_works
    verity_work
     verity_verify_io
      verity_hash_for_block
       verity_verify_level
        dm_bufio_read_with_ioprio
         new_read
          __bufio_new
           alloc_buffer
            gfp_mask: GFP_NOIO | __GFP_NORETRY | __GFP_NOMEMALLOC | __GFP_NOWARN

So the NOIO use itself is correct; the problem is on the reclaim side.

Here is the full picture of one such direct reclaim. It runs two rounds
of do_try_to_free_pages(); the target is 32 folios.

Round 1 - partial (shared) memcg walk, 169.20 ms, 0 folios reclaimed
--------------------------------------------------------------------
  prio 12->1 (~1.3 ms):
    cache_trim_mode is on, so get_scan_count() picks SCAN_FILE. Only the
    file side is scanned. Because this is a shared/partial walk, each
    priority only visits a handful of memcgs before the iterator is
    handed off, so very few memcgs are looked at on the way down:
    428 file folios scanned, 0 reclaimed.

  prio 0 (~167.9 ms):
    priority hits 0 without meeting the target, so get_scan_count()
    forces SCAN_EQUAL. The walk lands on a single memcg with a large,
    unswapped anon LRU and a tiny file LRU:

      inactive_anon ~335 MB, inactive_file ~4 MB   (~84:1)
      memcg swap usage ~3.6 MB, so swapcache is negligible

    shrink_lruvec() now keeps feeding that huge anon list into
    shrink_folio_list() - ~2400 shrink_folio_list() calls, ~93,000 anon
    folios scanned - and every folio hits the !__GFP_IO keep_locked path
    (not in swapcache, needs a swap slot). This single shrink_lruvec()
    pass alone is ~168 ms with 0 folios reclaimed.

  Round 1 ends with nr_reclaimed = 0 < target, so reclaim retries with
  sc->memcg_full_walk = 1.

Round 2 - full memcg walk, 2.37 ms, 68 folios reclaimed
-------------------------------------------------------
  With memcg_full_walk = 1, priority resets to 12 and every priority
  now visits the complete subtree (~78 memcgs). Progress is made
  entirely from the file side:

    prio 12: ...  0 reclaimed
    prio 11: ...  0
    prio 10: ...  3
    prio  9: ...  8
    prio  8: ... 18
    prio  7: ... 38   -> cumulative 68 >= target 32, done

  All 68 reclaimed folios come from file LRUs; anon contributes 0.

So the whole 168 ms is spent scanning an anon list that cannot yield a
single folio under GFP_NOIO, and the actual progress comes from file in
a fast full-walk round that follows.

> 150ms sounds awful indeed. Is this cumulative for a whole reclaim
> cycle or single shrink_folio_list() runs?

It is a single shrink_lruvec() invocation on that one memcg, as above -
not accumulated across the cycle. Each shrink_folio_list() only handles
SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX folios and is fast on its own; it's the prio-0 while
loop over the huge anon list that adds up to ~168 ms.

On the aging trade-off
----------------------
I take your point that this pass would otherwise have aged anon for the
next __GFP_IO reclaimer. But in this cycle that benefit is small and the
cost is large:

- The aging is not lost so much as deferred. Round 2 (and any later
  __GFP_IO reclaimer) still walks the full subtree; anon that genuinely
  needs IO to be reclaimed gets aged/reclaimed then, once IO is allowed.
- The 168 ms is spent scanning ~93k anon folios that, by construction of
  GFP_NOIO + negligible swapcache, cannot be reclaimed on this pass at
  all - the aging is the only product, and it comes at the price of a
  ~168 ms stall in a latency-sensitive path.

That's why I'd argue the balance tips towards skipping anon here rather
than aging it. To keep the change narrow, the check only triggers at
priority 0 (where SCAN_EQUAL is forced) and only when swapcache is far
below the anon LRU (below min(anon >> 6, SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX)), i.e. when
essentially no anon on the list is reclaimable without IO. Outside that
corner anon is scanned and aged exactly as before.

And skipping anon in this corner doesn't cost us the aging in practice:
with no reclaimable anon left to scan, Round 1 simply finishes quickly
and reclaim proceeds to the full-walk retry (Round 2), which resets to
priority 12 and walks the whole subtree - anon included - so anon still
gets aged there, just without the ~168 ms detour first.

Thanks,
Bo

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/5] mm: let folio_mkclean() report which pages had dirty PTEs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function, folio_mkclean_dirtymap(), which reports the pages of a folio that had dirty PTEs during the clearing process. The existing folio_mkclean() function is modified to use this new function and pass no bitmap, maintaining its original behavior. This change allows for more accurate tracking of page modifications in large folios, where only the per-entry dirty bit was previously recorded.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/5] mm: add a_ops->dirty_folio_range() and use the mkclean dirty harvest
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new operations to the Linux kernel: `a_ops->dirty_folio_range()` and `folio_mark_dirty_range()`. These operations allow a filesystem to mark only specific ranges of a folio as dirty, rather than the entire folio. The patch also updates the `folio_clear_dirty_for_io()` function to use these new operations instead of marking the whole folio dirty. This change is intended to improve performance by reducing unnecessary writes and allowing filesystems to track dirty state more accurately.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/5] mm: keep the mmap dirty range down to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the Linux kernel handles dirty ranges in memory mappings. It reduces the dirty range to a single page when only that page is written, rather than marking the entire folio as dirty. This change improves performance by avoiding unnecessary work and reducing the number of faults that occur due to incorrect dirty state. The patch addresses two specific issues: one where a shared mapping's folio was being marked dirty unnecessarily, and another where a batch of pages was being marked dirty on a write fault, even if only some of those pages were actually written to. The change is made in the `fault_dirty_shared_page` and `set_pte_range` functions, which are responsible for handling faults and page table updates.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/5] iomap: narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the iomap code to narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to only the faulting page, rather than the entire folio. It introduces a new function iomap_dirty_folio_range() that allows for more precise control over which parts of a folio are marked as dirty. The buffered write path and the mmap path now set the dirty range differently, with the latter setting everything due to the whole-folio coverage by iomap_dirty_folio(). The patch also updates several functions to use the new function and corrects some inconsistencies in the code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/5] xfs: track mmap dirty state per block
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the XFS file system to track the dirty state of memory-mapped blocks individually, rather than at the folio (2M) level. This change is made possible by replacing the `dirty_folio` operation with a new `dirty_folio_range` operation that allows for more precise tracking of dirty blocks. As a result, when writing data to a shared mapping, only the affected block is written back instead of the entire folio.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This RFC patch series proposes a new approach to tracking dirty state for PTE-mapped mmap writes, which currently dirties the entire folio even if only a subset of pages is written. The proposed solution harvests the hardware's record of which parts of the folio were written through a mapping and hands the filesystem the runs that were dirty. This is achieved by modifying the iomap_writeback_folio() function to submit only the dirty ranges and adding a new a_ops->dirty_folio_range() interface.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/2] iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Default queue depths to one page in a kdump kernel

By defaulting the queue depths to one page when is_kdump_kernel() returns true, the patch aims to conserve memory without impacting dump throughput. The change does not affect devices used for saving the dump or those that are switched off outright. An explicit cmdq_entries parameter still allows a capture kernel to request a deeper command queue if needed.

there. FWIW I've also used Claude to counter-check the report.

Summary: no code change appears to be needed for classes 1 and 2.
I should do test and module teardown fixes, as well as overflow cleanup
for a v22.

* Class 1: the supposed "over vs under" swapped accuracy bounds. In that
case it appears to be the LLM which is confused. This is because the range
of approximation as a function of the precise sum is expressed in the
opposite direction than the range of precise sum as a function of the
approximation:

+ * The range of the approximation as a function of the precise sum is expressed as:
+ *
+ *   approx_sum >= precise_sum - approx_accuracy_range.under
+ *   approx_sum <= precise_sum + approx_accuracy_range.over
+ *
+ * Therefore, the range of the precise sum as a function of the approximation is expressed as:
+ *
+ *   precise_sum <= approx_sum + approx_accuracy_range.under
+ *   precise_sum >= approx_sum - approx_accuracy_range.over

We could possibly extend this documentation elsewhere to make sure that a
LLM with limited context don't get confused, but the code is OK there.

Sashiko wrote that the positive margin "should be over_a + under_b" and then
claimed the code passes under_a + over_b. The code passes a->over + b->under.
Exactly what Sashiko itself derived. Its reasoning agreed with the code; it
misread which argument was which.

* Class 2:

> +void percpu_counter_tree_add(struct percpu_counter_tree *counter, long inc)
> +{
> +    unsigned long bit_mask = counter->level0_bit_mask, orig, res;
> +
> +    res = this_cpu_add_return(*counter->level0, inc);
> +    orig = res - inc;
> +    inc = percpu_counter_tree_carry(orig, res, inc, bit_mask);
> +    if (likely(!inc))
> +        return;
> +    percpu_counter_tree_add_slowpath(counter, inc);
> +}

Sashiko:
Does this code risk an unbounded approximation error if preemption occurs
after this_cpu_add_return() but before percpu_counter_tree_add_slowpath()?
The level 0 counter reflects the addition immediately, but if the task is
preempted before propagating the carry to the tree, that carry is held back
indefinitely. Multiple preempted tasks could cause the approximate sum to
deviate from the precise sum by an amount far exceeding the topological
accuracy bounds. Could we disable preemption across this entire sequence?

My take on this:

I think we need a clearer _documentation_ statement about what the approximation
upper bounds guarantee. It guarantees upper bounds on the approximation error
_when the counters are quiescent_, never when they are actively being concurrently
updated. So if a thread is preempted _while propagating the carry_, it's not
quiescent. I don't think we need any code change there. And disabling preemption
would not "fix" anything there, it would merely make the race smaller.


* Class 3:

Test cases boilerplate, module teardown and cpu hotplug issues: Good catches,
I'll fix them.

* Class 4: Overflows

In order to be strictly C compliant, I should do the difference in unsigned
(where overflow/underflow is OK), and cast the result as signed to compare
with 0 with a inequality. It won't change things in practice, but it's a good
call.

Thoughts ?

Thanks,

Mathieu

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] lib/zstd: add fallback aliases for disabled BMI2 variants
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds fallback aliases for disabled BMI2 variants in the Zstandard library. When dynamic BMI2 dispatch is disabled, the BMI2-specific functions are not compiled, but their names still need to be referenced. The patch introduces aliases that map these unavailable function names to their default implementations, allowing the code to compile without emitting BMI2-specific code. This change does not modify any existing code generation and only adds new aliases for future use.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] zstd: use cpu_feature_enabled() for in-kernel BMI2 dispatch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the performance of Zstandard (ZSTD) compression and decompression in the Linux kernel by using CPU feature checks to enable BMI2 instructions at runtime, rather than relying on static CPUID probing. The patch introduces a new abstraction for context initialization and uses x86 feature policy to allow x86 alternatives to resolve feature checks at boot time. This change improves performance by reducing the number of branches and allowing the CPU to optimize instruction sequences. Benchmarks show a 19.5% reduction in compression time and a 72.3% reduction in decompression time.
